932.title: Mira's treasure
932.hook: a woman who left a palace counts her treasure: the name of God
932.carry: the name of God is the real treasure
932.tomorrow: Chaitanya takes the names to the street
932.howItsDone: Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo is sung as a bhajan at home gatherings, in temples and on concert stages, and many Hindus practice japa, repeating a name of God on a mala of 108 beads.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mira sang, belonging to God loosens the world's shame, and no one else, and the world's shame lost its grip.
screen: `MIRABAI'S SONGS.` · `BELONGING TO GOD LOOSENS THE WORLD'S SHAME.`

segments.voice: A strange inventory for a princess. Mira grew up, the stories say, among jewels and silks, in a house with a treasury. She walked away from all of it. And one of the songs sung in her voice is about getting rich. Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo. I've found it, I've found the treasure, the jewel of Ram's name. A woman who left a royal house describes what she has now in the language of money.
screen: `JEWELS, SILKS, A TREASURY.` → `SHE WALKS AWAY.` → `I'VE FOUND THE TREASURE.`

segments.voice: Listen to it like a bank statement. Credit: a priceless thing, given to me by my true guru, out of kindness. Balance: the savings of lifetime after lifetime, found at last. Then come terms no bank has ever offered. Spend it, and it doesn't run down. Thieves can't touch it. Day by day it grows. Then the song leaves the bank for a river. The boat is truth, the boatman is the true guru, and I have crossed the ocean of becoming. The last line: Mira's lord is Giridhar, and she sings his praise with joy upon joy. So what is the treasure? Not a thing. A name. This is one of the great teachings of bhakti: the name of God, nama, isn't a label stuck on the treasure. For the bhakti saints, saying the name is how you hold it. That's why so many Hindus repeat a name of God, softly, again and again, often on a mala, a string of a hundred and eight beads. It's called japa. Notice the names here, too. Mira's beloved is Krishna, the mountain-lifter, yet she sings of the jewel of Ram's name. Some readers hear Ram's name here as the name of God itself, and the song holds both names without strain. And the treasure is given, not earned: a guru hands it over in kindness. So a woman who lost a palace counts herself rich, because the name of God is the one thing that grows when it's spent.

segments.voice: Today, try japa, the practice this song is about. Choose a name of God your family uses, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, the Mother, or simply Om, and say it softly, once with each slow breath. If you have a mala, move one bead for each name; if not, count on your fingers. Notice that saying it doesn't use anything up. If you don't pray, repeat one word that holds what you love most, and let it be your treasure for a minute.
Mirabai's songs. In this one, the jewel of the name: a treasure no thief can steal, which grows each day it's spent.

933.title: Chaitanya takes the names to the street
933.hook: a grammar teacher whose every lesson turns into Krishna
933.carry: kirtan: god's names, a song anyone can join
933.tomorrow: Humbler than a blade of grass
933.howItsDone: In Gaudiya Vaishnava temples and homes, kirtan is sung with drums and hand cymbals, one voice leading and the group answering, and street processions of chanting, called nagar kirtan, still pass through towns and cities.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mira's jewel of the name. The name of God is the real treasure, and it grows when it's spent.
screen: `MIRA'S TREASURE.` · `THE NAME OF GOD IS THE REAL TREASURE.`

segments.voice: A grammar teacher in Bengal has a problem. His students come to learn Sanskrit grammar, and every rule he explains turns into Krishna. A verb ending? Krishna. A noun? One of Krishna's names. Tradition says this young teacher, Nimai, was known in his town of Navadvipa as a brilliant scholar and a fierce debater. Then he went on pilgrimage to Gaya, and came home unable to talk about anything else. His students, the story goes, closed their books and left. He let them go. He had found something louder than grammar.
screen: `A GRAMMAR TEACHER IN BENGAL.` → `EVERY RULE TURNS INTO KRISHNA.` → `THE STUDENTS CLOSE THEIR BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Nimai is the man remembered as Chaitanya. Back home, he and his friends began to gather at night in the courtyard of a devotee named Shrivasa, doors shut, singing God's names together. Drums, cymbals, one voice leading, everyone answering. That's kirtan: praise sung out loud, together, the names repeated again and again. Then the doors opened. Chaitanya's companions took the singing into the lanes of Navadvipa, a procession moving from house to house, and whoever heard it could fall in behind. At its center his tradition places one chant: Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Nothing but names, calling and calling. His tradition teaches that in this age, the Kali Yuga, singing the names of God is the surest path of all. What's radical is how little it asks. No Sanskrit grammar, no years of study, no temple door to get through. You need a voice, or even just ears and the willingness to answer. His followers in Bengal, the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, remember him dancing as he sang, weeping, falling to the ground, his whole body caught up in the names. They also hold that he was more than a saint: Krishna himself, joined with Radha, come to taste his own love from the inside. Others honor him as a great teacher of devotion. Either way, what he gave the street was the same: a song anyone could join on the first try.
screen: `NIGHTS IN SHRIVASA'S COURTYARD.` · `THE DOORS OPEN TO THE LANES.` · `NOTHING BUT NAMES.` · `THE PATH FOR THIS AGE.` · then, large: `A SONG ANYONE CAN JOIN.`

segments.voice: Kirtan is a call and an answer, so try it. Say a name of God softly, the leader's line: Hari, or Krishna, or Rama, or a name your family uses. Then answer it yourself, a little more softly, the way the crowd would. Keep the call and the answer going, gently, for a few rounds; that's how kirtan begins. If you don't pray, call and answer with one soft sound, and notice how easy it is to join.
Kirtan. Praise sung aloud, God's names repeated together with drums and cymbals, which Chaitanya took out of a closed courtyard and into the street.
screen: `KIRTAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: kirtan, God's names, a song anyone can join. All it asks is a voice, or even just ears. Until tomorrow.

934.title: Humbler than a blade of grass
934.hook: humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree
934.carry: humbler than grass, you can sing the name always
934.howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas recite the Shikshashtakam, and the grass-and-tree verse is often sung or quoted before kirtan; at Puri's Ratha Yatra, kirtan groups sing and dance before Jagannath's chariot.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: kirtan. Chaitanya took God's names into the street, kirtan: god's names, a song anyone can join.
screen: `KIRTAN.` · `GOD'S NAMES, KIRTAN: GOD'S NAMES, A SONG ANYONE CAN JOIN.`

segments.voice: Step on a blade of grass and it bends flat. Lift your foot and, after a moment, it stands back up. No complaint, no grudge. A tree stands in the sun all day and gives its shade to whoever sits down, even the one with the axe. Those two humble things, grass and a tree, open a short verse that Chaitanya's tradition treasures. On the last day with the saints of bhakti, it answers a practical question: how do you keep singing?
screen: `GRASS BENDS, THEN STANDS.` → `A TREE GIVES ITS SHADE.` → `HOW DO YOU KEEP SINGING?`

segments.voice: Chaitanya's followers keep a short set of verses under his name, called the Shikshashtakam, his teaching. One goes, in plain English: be humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree. Give honor to others, and ask none for yourself. Then you can sing the name of Hari always. This is how his tradition teaches humility: not as feeling small, but as the condition for staying with God's name. Read it as the fine print under kirtan. Anyone can join the song on the first try. Staying in it is harder. Pride wants the lead line. Impatience wants the song to end. Wanting respect turns a chorus into a competition. The verse clears all three away, and what's left can keep singing. His tradition remembers him living it out in Puri, on the coast, where he spent his later years near the temple of Jagannath. At the great chariot festival, the Ratha Yatra, he's remembered dancing before the rolling chariot with groups of kirtan singers, lost in the names, the whole crowd caught up with him. Now look back over these four weeks. Andal and Nammalvar, singing to Vishnu in Tamil. The Nayanars, singing to Shiva. Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram, walking and singing in Maharashtra. Kabir and his sharp couplets. Tulsidas and Hanuman's song. Surdas in Yashoda's yard. Mira, laughing over the cup. And Chaitanya in the street with a drum. Different languages, different names for God. One habit: they sang to God as if God were near.
screen: `HUMBLER THAN GRASS.` · `MORE PATIENT THAN A TREE.` · `DANCING BEFORE THE CHARIOT.` · then, large: `THEY SANG AS IF GOD WERE NEAR.`

segments.voice: Many Gaudiya Vaishnavas say this verse before they chant, so try it that way. Say it slowly in your own words: humbler than grass, more patient than a tree, giving honor and asking none. Let go of one small need to be right or to be noticed. Then say a name of God, Hari, Krishna, or the name you use, a few times, gently. If you don't pray, say the verse, and bring to mind one person you could honor today without needing anything back.
Shikshashtakam. Chaitanya's short teaching verses, the fine print that keeps the song going: humbler than grass, more patient than a tree.

segments.voice: Your line: humbler than grass, you can sing the name always. Next come the modern teachers, starting with a temple priest near Calcutta. See you tomorrow.

935.title: Who weeps for God?
935.hook: a schoolteacher with a notebook, and a priest who asks who weeps for God
935.carry: long for god the way lungs want air
935.tomorrow: The snake that was told not to bite
935.howItsDone: The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna is read aloud in study circles and at Ramakrishna centers, and devotees visit the temple garden at Dakshineswar, where his room is kept.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chaitanya's verse. humbler than grass, you can sing the name always, more patient than a tree, and you can sing the name always.
screen: `HUMBLER THAN A BLADE OF GRASS.` · `SING THE NAME ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: A schoolteacher keeps a diary. That sounds like nothing. But this one comes home from visits to a temple garden north of Calcutta and writes down, as exactly as he can, what a priest there said that day: the jokes, the songs, the questions, who was sitting in the room. He signs his work with a single letter: M. Those pages became a book in Bengali, the Kathamrita, and in English, the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna. The modern teachers begin with the man in that room.
screen: `A SCHOOLTEACHER KEEPS A DIARY.` → `HE SIGNS IT: M.` → `THE MAN IN THAT ROOM.`

segments.voice: Ramakrishna served as a priest at the Kali temple at Dakshineswar, on the bank of the Ganges. The stories about him keep returning to one thing: he longed for God, for the Divine Mother, with an intensity that alarmed the people around him. Tradition says that as a young priest he would weep at the end of a day: another day gone, Mother, and still you haven't shown yourself. Years later, with visitors from the city in his room, he kept coming back to that longing. In the Gospel he says, in effect: people shed jugs of tears over their wives and children, over money and property. Who weeps for God? And he tells a story. A disciple asked his teacher how to see God. Come with me, the teacher said, walked him to a pond, and pushed his head under the water. Held it there. Then let him up, gasping. What did you feel? I felt I'd die for one breath of air. When you long for God like that, the teacher said, you will see God. It isn't a method; nobody is being told to hold anyone's head under water. It's a measurement: how much do you want this? Not cleverness first, not learning first. Wanting God the way lungs want air. This is the heart of bhakti as Ramakrishna taught it: longing for God, which teachers in his tradition call vyakulata, a restless yearning, matters more than learning. Cry to God with a longing heart, he told his visitors, and you will see God.
screen: `A PRIEST AT DAKSHINESWAR.` · `WHO WEEPS FOR GOD?` · `A HEAD HELD UNDER WATER.` · `VYAKULATA: LONGING FOR GOD.` · then, large: `WANT GOD THE WAY LUNGS WANT AIR.`

segments.voice: Ramakrishna's advice was simple: find a quiet corner and call to God the way a child calls for its mother. Try it now, silently or in a whisper, in your own words: tell God what you long for most, honestly, not politely. If you pray to the Mother, or Krishna, or Shiva, use that name. If you don't pray, name the thing you want most underneath everything, and rest with that wanting for a few slow breaths.
Ramakrishna. The priest of the Kali temple at Dakshineswar, whose conversations M. wrote down, and who asked: who weeps for God?

segments.voice: Your line: long for God the way lungs want air. In these sayings, longing comes before cleverness. Day nine hundred thirty-five, done.

936.title: The snake that was told not to bite
936.hook: a snake promises not to bite, and the village boys find out
936.carry: ahimsa: never bite, but you may hiss
936.tomorrow: The salt doll and the ocean
936.howItsDone: Ramakrishna's parables, like the snake that was told not to bite, are retold in talks and study circles at Ramakrishna Math and Mission centers, often as practical guidance for people living family lives.

segments.voice: A village path has a problem: a snake lives beside it, and it bites. People take the long way around. Then a holy man comes walking down that path, unafraid, and the snake rises to strike. He calms it with a few words and gives it a teaching. Ramakrishna told this story in his room at Dakshineswar to visitors who lived ordinary lives, with jobs, families and difficult neighbors. It's a funny story, with a serious point.
screen: `A SNAKE BY THE VILLAGE PATH.` → `A HOLY MAN, UNAFRAID.` → `A TEACHING FOR A SNAKE.`

segments.voice: The holy man gives the snake a sacred name to repeat and tells it: stop biting. Harm no one. That's ahimsa, non-harm, the first of the yamas that open the Yoga Sutras' eight limbs, and one of the oldest ideals in Hinduism. The snake takes it to heart, and stops. Soon the cowherd boys of the village notice the dangerous snake is harmless now. They throw stones at it. They grab it by the tail, whirl it around and dash it on the ground. The snake drags itself, half dead, into its hole, and grows thin, barely eating. Later the holy man comes back and finds his disciple, bruised and thin. What happened to you? You told me not to bite, the snake says. So I didn't. And look at me. The holy man answers: I told you not to bite. I never told you not to hiss. Ramakrishna draws it out for the people in the room. Someone living in the world, he says, should harm no one. But they may need to raise a hiss, so that others don't take advantage. Many teachers read this as a line drawn inside ahimsa itself. Non-harm is about what you do to others: no bite, no venom, no wish to wound. It was never a vow to let yourself, or the people in your care, be destroyed. He gives this parable to householders, people with offices, families and neighbors who push, whose dharma includes protecting what's been put in their hands. The hiss isn't the bite.

937.title: The salt doll and the ocean
937.hook: a doll made of salt walks into the sea to measure how deep it is
937.carry: brahman is known by melting, not measuring
937.howItsDone: Devotees read the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna in study circles and at centers of the Ramakrishna order, and his parables, like the salt doll, are retold in talks and at home.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna's snake, told to stop biting, and the holy man's line: ahimsa: never bite, but you may hiss. Ahimsa: never bite, but you may hiss.

segments.voice: A doll made entirely of salt sets out to measure the ocean. Small doll, big job: find out how deep the water goes, then come back and report. It walks down to the shore and steps in. And right there the story stops being about measuring, because the moment the doll is in the water, it starts to dissolve. Ramakrishna told this little parable when people asked him a question that sounds simple: what is God like, really?
screen: `A DOLL MADE OF SALT.` → `IT GOES TO MEASURE THE OCEAN.` → `IT NEVER COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: His visitors were often educated men, used to debating. They wanted a definition. He gave them pictures instead, and the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, the book of his conversations, is full of them. The salt doll went to measure the ocean, and it melted. So who was left to come back and say how deep it was? That is his answer about Brahman, the reality the Upanishads point to beyond every name. You can't stand outside it and take its measurements, because the one measuring is made of the same stuff. Get close enough, and the measurer is gone. He makes the same point another way, and it's startling. Everything, he says, has become uchchhishta, food that has already been tasted: leftovers. The Vedas, the scriptures, the philosophies have all passed through human mouths. Only Brahman has never been made leftover, because no one has ever been able to say what it is. Notice what he isn't saying. He isn't throwing scripture away. He sang hymns, quoted the sacred books, and worshiped the Mother in the temple. Words point, and what they point to is bigger than any mouth. And the parable isn't a sad one. The doll goes in because it wants to know. Many readers hear in it the Upanishads' great teaching that atman, your deepest self, and Brahman are not two: a doll of salt came from the sea in the first place. Its not coming back is the answer.
screen: `THE SALT DOLL MELTS.` · `NO ONE COMES BACK TO REPORT.` · `EVERYTHING ELSE IS LEFTOVERS.` · `WORDS POINT; THEY DON'T CONTAIN.` · then, large: `ATMAN AND BRAHMAN: NOT TWO.`

Try silently to describe it in one sentence, and notice how the sentence falls short. Then let the sentence go, and simply stay near the thing itself, the way the doll stood at the water's edge.

938.title: The chameleon on the tree

segments.voice: Red. I saw it myself, it was red. No, it was green, I was standing right there. You're both wrong, it was blue. Three friends, one tree, one small lizard, and an argument getting louder by the minute. Each of them went into the woods, saw a chameleon on a branch, and came back certain. Ramakrishna told this story to the visitors in his room at Dakshineswar, and the one who settles it isn't any of the three.
screen: `RED.` → `NO, GREEN.` → `NO, BLUE.`

segments.voice: In the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, they all walk back to the tree to settle it. A man sitting underneath says: I live here, and I know that creature well. Every one of you is right. Sometimes it's red, sometimes green, sometimes yellow or blue. And sometimes it has no color at all. Ramakrishna gives the meaning plainly. The one who thinks of God constantly comes to know God's real nature, and knows that God shows himself to seekers in many forms and aspects: with qualities, and then again without any. Hindus have names for both. Saguna: God with qualities, the Krishna you can dress, feed and sing to. Nirguna: God beyond every quality and every name. Ramakrishna wouldn't let either side throw out the other. It's the others, he says, who suffer through useless arguments. Notice what the man under the tree does not say. He doesn't tell anyone they made it up. Each friend really did see red, or green. The trouble came with one extra word: only. And his knowledge comes not from a sharper argument but from living there: closeness, not cleverness. His last words, sometimes no color at all, point to where the doll went. That closes a week. It began with Mira's jewel of the name, went out into the lanes of Bengal with Chaitanya's drums, and came to rest at Dakshineswar, where a priest answered questions with a pond, a snake, a doll made of salt, and a lizard on a tree.
screen: `THE MAN UNDER THE TREE.` · `EVERY ONE OF YOU IS RIGHT.` · `SAGUNA AND NIRGUNA.` · `SOMETIMES NO COLOR AT ALL.` · `CLOSENESS, NOT CLEVERNESS.`

segments.voice: Pray today to God in the form you love: a picture or murti of Krishna, Shiva or the Mother, or a name, if that's your way. Then close your eyes and rest a moment in the silence beyond the picture, the part with no color at all. Then bring to mind someone who sees God differently from you, and ask quietly what they saw from where they were standing. If you don't pray, do the last part only.
Ramakrishna. The priest of Dakshineswar, telling of a lizard on a tree that shows every color, and sometimes no color at all.
